summary: Count the groups of mutually connected cities given an adjacency matrix.
mainInsight: Provinces are the connected components of the graph. Run DFS/BFS from every unvisited city and count the number of searches started; union-find gives the same answer.

approaches.name: DFS over the adjacency matrix
approaches.summary: dfs(i): for j with isConnected[i][j] unvisited, recurse.

approaches.name: Build an adjacency list then DFS

personalSolution.approach: Build an adjacency list, then DFS per component
personalSolution.notes: Correct. DFS directly on the matrix avoids the O(n^2) adjacency list.

cards.answer: Count connected components of the graph given as an adjacency matrix (DFS/BFS from each unvisited city, or union-find). Clue: Direct or indirect connection groups cities into provinces, which are the connected components of the graph, so count traversals or unions.

cards.explanation: Indirect connections are transitive, so each group is a connected component and one traversal covers it.

promptVariants: What graph concept does Number of Provinces ask for?
options: Connected components via DFS/BFS or union-find
Shortest paths between each pair of provinces
Topological order of the cities in the graph
Minimum spanning tree of the connected cities
cards.answer: Connected components via DFS/BFS or union-find
cards.explanation: A province is a group of cities connected directly or indirectly.

promptVariants: Why does each DFS start correspond to exactly one province?
What marks a city as belonging to a counted province?
cards.answer: A DFS from a city visits every city reachable from it, i.e. its whole component, and marks them visited. Any later unvisited city must belong to a different component, so the number of DFS starts equals the number of components.

promptVariants: Time complexity with an n x n matrix: ___
Complete the statement: Time complexity with an n x n matrix: ___
cards.explanation: Each matrix entry is examined a constant number of times.

promptVariants: What do the adjacency list and the visited set cost compared with DFS directly on the matrix?
Compare the memory of building an adjacency list with running DFS directly on the matrix.
cards.answer: The adjacency list costs O(n^2) in the worst case (dense graph), the visited set O(n), and recursion O(n). DFS directly on the matrix needs only O(n) (visited + recursion).

promptVariants: Why does `for node in graph.keys()` visit every city even though isolated cities exist?
What is the role of the diagonal entries?
cards.answer: The diagonal isConnected[i][i] is 1 (every city is connected to itself), so every city gets at least one entry and appears in graph.keys(). Without that guarantee isolated cities would be missed; looping `for node in range(n)` is the robust choice.
keyPoints: Diagonal makes every city a key
cards.explanation: Self-loops are harmless for DFS with a visited set.

promptVariants: What is the answer when only the diagonal of a 4 x 4 matrix is 1?
How many provinces if no cities are connected?
cards.explanation: With only the diagonal set every city is isolated, so each city is its own province.

incorrectOptionExplanations.1: One province would need every city to be connected.
incorrectOptionExplanations.0: There are cities, so at least one province exists.
incorrectOptionExplanations.16: 16 is the number of matrix cells, not provinces.
